items.text: Selection methods · Fetchers · Spiders · Proxy Rotation · CLI · MCP Scrapling is a Python Web Scraping framework that brings fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, powerful parsing, and concurrent crawling into one library. Scrape static pages, render JavaScript, interact with websites, and extract data from the API calls behind them. Build crawlers with reusable sessions, proxy rotation, automatic retries, pause/resume, and built-in data exports. Use it from Python, the terminal, or your AI agent through its MCP server and Agent Skill. From extracting a few fields to collecting a whole website as clean Markdown, Scrapling covers the full scraping workflow. - Fetch & interact: Fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, JavaScript rendering, Cloudflare Turnstile/Interstitial handling, persistent sessions, and background API capture. - Parse & extract: CSS, XPath, text and regex search, adaptive element tracking, similar-element matching, and clean Markdown output. - Crawl & export: Concurrent spiders, proxy rotation, retries, AutoThrottle, pause/resume, streaming, ready-made templates, and JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exports. - Scrape with AI or from your terminal: An MCP server for AI agents to browse and extract data, an Agent Skill, CLI commands, and an interactive shell. Start with a single page: from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/') quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall() print(quotes) Or scale up with a spider: from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Response class QuotesSpider(Spider): name = "quotes" start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"] async def parse(self, response: Response): for quote in response.css('.quote'): yield { "text": quote.css('.text::text').get(), "author": quote.css('.author::text').get(), } res...

items.text: 让 AI Agent 够得着它自己上不去的互联网 登录墙后的平台、视频里的内容、中文平台、干净的结构化数据，一条命令拿到 💬 有问题、想要新平台、或者想看看别人怎么用？来 Discord 聊聊。 点击展开 Agent Reach 让你的 Agent 真正连上互联网，用上它自己够不着的平台和能力。 Claude Code、Codex、Hermes Agent、OpenClaw 这类 CLI Agent 自带搜索和网页读取，但下面这些它们基本够不着： - 要登录才能用的功能：在小红书搜笔记、在 X 查账号动态、读职位详情等。 - 视频里的内容：B站和 YouTube 的字幕，以及 YouTube 视频、小宇宙播客的语音转文字。 - 中文平台：B站、小红书、V2EX、雪球，通用搜索覆盖很差。 - 干净的结构化数据：雪球行情、V2EX 帖子和回复、GitHub 仓库和 issue，拿到的是整理好的内容。 Agent Reach 把这些平台背后的工具替你装好、测好，Agent 一条命令就能用： agent-reach channels # 有哪些渠道、每个渠道能做什么 agent-reach bilibili search "大模型" # agent-reach [参数] agent-reach read https://www.v2ex.com/t/123 # 按链接自动选渠道 - 适用于哪些 Agent？ 一切 Agent 都能用。 - 会碰我的浏览器和账号吗？ 要登录的平台用 Agent Reach 自己的专用浏览器，在后台运行、不弹窗。第一次用某个网站时，会把你 Chrome 里这个网站的登录复制一份过去，原浏览器不变，不读密码库。复制过来的通常是主账号，建议换成小号，做法见下面的"安全性"。详见会话配置。 下表是当前版本的情况。 - 默认：装好就能用；不想要也可以去掉，以后更新不会再加回来。 - 可选：说一句"帮我加上 XX"就开启，需要的软件会自动装好。 - 实验：能用，但平台反爬更严，可能随时失效。 把这句话发给你的 Agent： 帮我安装 Agent Reach：https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/Agent-Reach/main/docs/install.md 无论是安装还是升级，都只需要这一条命令就行了。 剩下的 Agent 自己做完。过程中你可能会被问到： - 允许它执行命令：如果 Agent 说自己不能运行命令，去它的设置里打开"允许执行命令"。 - 装 uv：uv 是一个安装命令行程序的小工具，不需要管理员密码。电脑上没有的话 Agent 会先装它，会跟你说一声。 - 要不要加可选渠道：装完后 Agent 会告诉你哪些已经能用（B站、V2EX、GitHub、YouTube、网页），以及还能加哪些。你选了再加，也可以以后随时说"帮我加上小红书"，一条命令就装好。 关于登录：部分平台会直接复用你电脑上已有的登录。想换成某个特定账号（比如小号），跟 Agent 说一声就行。Agent 从不替你登录，也不会要你的密码。 ⚠️ PyPI 上叫agent-reach 的包不是本项目，请勿从 PyPI 安装，只用 install.md 里的 GitHub 地址。 Agent Reach 装的所有东西（各渠道的工具、登录、设置）都放在你电脑上同一个文件夹里（~/.agent-reach/ ），不散落到别处。所以升级、管理、删除都很省事，一句话就行。 直接用大白话跟 Agent 说： 出了问题，Agent 会告诉你是哪个平台、什么原因、下一步怎么做。常见问题见 troubleshooting.md。 每个平台的每个动作都有一个按顺序尝试的工具列表。比如读 B站视频先用 bili-cli，失败了自动换 B站公开接口；读网页先用 Jina Reader，再用 Exa。 flowchart LR A[Agent] -->|agent-reach 渠道 动作| B[Agent Reach] B --> C{按顺序尝试} C -->|首选| D[上游工具 1] C -->|失败时备选| E[上游工具 2] D --> F[结果] E --> F F --> A 平台改版、工具失效是常态。换工...

items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.summary: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: - Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible - Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it - Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship GitHub is built for developers and their agents. items.text: GitLab security incident: attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-97229 On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with. GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with “Forgot your password?” on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites. If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org. What happened The vulnerability: CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12, but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23, in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9. items.text: Senior Software Engineer Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: - Minimize coordination - Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. items.title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
items.summary: Comments
items.text: I can't believe it's not silicon Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide.) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever. To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage. I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring, and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with. You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope, and the code is on GitHub. The RNN inside Qwen3.5 can be exact RAM Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism (more on that here). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated. Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1,11 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. items.text: Preamble I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others). At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all? To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases. For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another. Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases. I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden. As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions. items.title: CNC Stone Carving
items.summary: Comments
items.text: CNC Stone Carving In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place. However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange. To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head. (The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.) CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church. Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days. Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today. The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth. Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers. The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God. What is a CNC machine CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine. The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts. Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention. Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone. The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away. items.title: The future of the firm
items.summary: How AI might enter the org chart—beneath, beside, and between us.
items.text: How AI might enter the org chart—beneath, beside, and between us. By Hemanth Asirvatham and Elliott Mokski Loading… Authors’ note: This is the second essay in our series on the next economy, part of a new platform to host independent voices exploring an AGI future. It reflects our views, not those of OpenAI or our colleagues. The two of us were twenty-four when we started managing our own teams here at OpenAI. That is less impressive once you meet our teams. We’re supposed to be grunts. At twenty-four, you’re at the bottom of the corporate ladder. You take the meeting notes and write a few memos. After years of drudgerous work, you are (hopefully) granted a broader remit. Our path—and the path of many young people today—is looking different. We enter the workforce already with “employees” at our behest. These deputies work day and night, weekends and holidays. They are great at the grunt work. We even have math olympiad gold medalists on staff to advise us. Our new reports still make their share of mistakes. But they are getting better, learning our needs, and we are learning how to manage them. Neither of us climbed the corporate ladder. Management has instead come down to our rung. This essay is about our promotion, and the other ways firms might reorganize as we enter the intelligence age. When AI enters the firm, where does it go? We present three illustrative scenarios: Beneath us. Everyone keeps their seat, and a new basement of AI labor grows underneath. We all become managers. First we get assistants, then chiefs of staff, and eventually entire miniature firms reporting up to each of us. Every person gets a promotion. Beside us. items.title: A Health Update
items.summary: Comments
items.text: I’m writing this post from a hospital bed. And I couldn’t be happier. You hear folks say chemotherapy sucks, but until you go through it yourself, you don’t really know how bad it can be. It remains a popular activity only because it’s better than the alternative. My first exposure to chemotherapy was with this contraption: a fluoroscope. Every week, they used this machine to tap into my spine, extract 5 mg of fluid for analysis, and replace it with 5 mg of methotrexate. There was only a local anesthetic during the procedure and the hardest part was knowing that there was a needle, turned up to eleven, going into my back. It was afterwards that things got dicey: the nerves in your spine float in a thecal sac filled with spinal fluid that acts as a kind of insulator. Since we were exchanging the fluids, it was easy for the levels to get out of balance and for the nerves to react. The result were the worst headaches I’ve ever experienced. The good news is that the remedy was simple: to lie flat on my back to ease the pressure gravity was putting on my spine. That was also the bad news: many days were spent lying prone and trying to avoid boredom. Watching shows and scrolling timelines just doesn’t cut it when that’s all you can do. Thankfully, the spinal headaches subsided quickly when the six-week course of lumbar punctures finished at the end of January. But my body began to face a new challenge: chemotherapy infusions of Bendamustine and Rituximab. Everyone experiences chemotherapy differently. Just as every body is different, so is the reaction to the chemicals that are killing the cancer.
